Citation checks on the draft found nothing fabricated or overruled in coverage, so I'm now finalizing the argument, with notes on what the tool couldn't verify.

**ARGUMENT**

**Plaintiff Waived Any Right to Compel Arbitration by Substantially Utilizing the Litigation Machinery.**

**A. Waiver turns on Plaintiff's own conduct; prejudice is not required.**

This Court long held that a litigant may waive its right to arbitrate "by so substantially utilizing the litigation machinery that to subsequently permit arbitration would prejudice the party opposing the stay." *MicroStrategy, Inc. v. Lauricia*, 268 F.3d 244, 249 (4th Cir. 2001) (quoting *Maxum Founds., Inc. v. Salus Corp.*, 779 F.2d 974, 981 (4th Cir. 1985)), *abrogated in part by Morgan v. Sundance, Inc.*, 596 U.S. 411 (2022). *Morgan* eliminated the prejudice requirement. Federal courts may not create arbitration-specific procedural rules, including a rule conditioning waiver on prejudice. 596 U.S. at 417–19. The waiver inquiry focuses on the conduct of the party that held the right and whether it knowingly relinquished that right by acting inconsistently with it. *Id.*

This Court's earlier decisions remain instructive on litigation conduct, but not insofar as they require prejudice or impose a heightened, arbitration-specific burden. Section 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act conditions a stay on the applicant's not being "in default in proceeding with such arbitration." 9 U.S.C. § 3. This Court has treated default as akin to waiver. *See Patten Grading & Paving, Inc. v. Skanska USA Bldg., Inc.*, 380 F.3d 200, 204–05 (4th Cir. 2004), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411; *Forrester v. Penn Lyon Homes, Inc.*, 553 F.3d 340, 342–43 (4th Cir. 2009), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411. Relevant considerations have included the length of delay and the extent of the movant's trial-oriented activity. *See Rota-McLarty v. Santander Consumer USA, Inc.*, 700 F.3d 690, 702–03 (4th Cir. 2012), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411; *Wheeling Hosp., Inc. v. Health Plan of the Upper Ohio Valley, Inc.*, 683 F.3d 577, 586–87 (4th Cir. 2012), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411.

**B. Plaintiff's litigation conduct is irreconcilable with an intent to arbitrate.**

Plaintiff chose this forum. It filed suit on [date] and did not seek arbitration until [date], [number] months later. In the interim, it [served written discovery; took depositions; filed merits motions; sought affirmative relief; agreed to a scheduling order and trial date]. [Record cites.] Each step used the judicial process to advance the very dispute Plaintiff now says belongs elsewhere.

*Degidio v. Crazy Horse Saloon & Restaurant Inc.*, 880 F.3d 135, 140–42 (4th Cir. 2018), is instructive. There, this Court affirmed the refusal to compel arbitration where the defendant had litigated the merits at length before pressing arbitration. A party should not be permitted to test the judicial forum and then switch to arbitration when that forum appears less promising. *See id.* Plaintiff attempted exactly that when it moved to compel only after [describe adverse ruling or development].

Decisions rejecting waiver do not rescue Plaintiff. *E.g.*, *MicroStrategy*, 268 F.3d at 249–54; *Am. Recovery Corp. v. Computerized Thermal Imaging, Inc.*, 96 F.3d 88, 95–96 (4th Cir. 1996), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411; *Rota-McLarty*, 700 F.3d at 702–04; *Forrester*, 553 F.3d at 342–44. Those decisions applied a standard requiring the opposing party to prove actual prejudice, the very condition *Morgan* rejects. Delay and litigation activity now matter for what they reveal about the conduct and intent of the party seeking arbitration.

**C. Defendant would prevail even under the former standard.**

Although unnecessary, prejudice is present. Defendant has spent [amount] litigating in court, disclosed [defense theories and evidence] through [discovery and motions], and suffered [other disadvantage]. [Record cites.] Compelling arbitration now would force Defendant to duplicate that effort after Plaintiff has obtained advantages that might have been unavailable in arbitration. Arbitration should not be compelled.

---

**Check before filing**

- **The assigned standard is outdated.** *Morgan* (2022) removed the prejudice element, so I argued waiver without it and kept prejudice only as an alternative.
- **Verification limits.** Redline confirmed that the seven F.3d citations exist and found no overruling. It still labels them "good law" because its Supreme Court data ends in 2014. *Morgan* and *Maxum* are outside its coverage and rest on my own knowledge.
- **Read the opinions.** The quotation, pin cites, case descriptions and abrogation signals are also from my knowledge; the tools did not check them. Confirm each, especially *Degidio* and *Wheeling*. Also check for Fourth Circuit waiver decisions after *Morgan*.
- **Posture.** I assumed Plaintiff is the party seeking arbitration, since we represent the defendant. If our client is the one moving to compel, this argument cuts against us. Adjust the final sentence to match the relief sought on appeal (affirm or reverse).
